newsitem.title: UK: Christmas-but no respite for troubled N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Christmas-but no respite for troubled N.Ireland.

text.p: Northern Ireland's battered peace process faced fresh unheaval on Tuesday as Christmas approached with no sign of a traditional IRA guerrilla truce and a ceasefire by their Loyalist foes apparently hanging by a thread.
It is the first time for six years that the beleaguered community has not been promised some respite from the threat of sectarian violence over the Christmas period.
A two-year peace drive is on the rocks, the Irish Republican Army has gone back to a bombing and shooting war and pro-British Loyalists are giving off warlike signals.
"Escalation in violence feared" headlined the Dublin Irish Times reporting that security services on both sides of the border are on high alert against possible IRA or Loyalist attacks.
"Slaughter on border fear", blared the Belfast Newsletter, reporting that "a Christmas crisis is threatening to end Ulster's fragile peace process".

At the height of hostilities over the past 25 years, the run-up to Christmas was often intensely violent as IRA "active service units" wreaked bombing and killing havoc in town centres and marauding Loyalist guerrilla squads terrorised Catholic areas in what they said were reprisal attacks.
But the Christmas holiday period from December 24 to 26 usually produced a lull as guerrillas on both sides stayed at home.

The IRA unofficially ceased hostilties for many years over Christmas but in 1991 it publicly announced a 72-hour ceasefire which it repeated annually until a "complete cessation" proclaimed in September 1994.

Loyalists, so-called because of an unswerving allegiance to British rule, also had unofficial Christmas ceasefires but in October 1994 they also announced they were laying down their weapons for good.
Business boomed, new hotels opened, tourism trade rocketed and Christmas shopping last year hit a high.
The province seemed to be on the brink of a fresh start aimed at overcoming deeply ingrained differences over British rule, but political efforts to cement the peace spun into a deadlock.
Last February, the IRA shattered peace hopes with bombs on mainland Britain.

A 72-hour period last weekend led to a rapid deterioration in the security climate. IRA gunmen caused outrage by entering a children's hospital and wounding the bodyguard of a Protestant politician who was visiting his seriously ill son.
On Sunday a senior Irish republican was wounded by a booby- trapped bomb in his car in an attack blamed on Loyalist guerrillas.
Protestant extremists have not commented and are refusing to say whether it marks the abandonment of their truce and a slide back into sectarian tit-for-tat violence.
